opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to think about it is as a new kind of collaborator, one that's available at any hour and has read more than any of us ever could, but that still needs you to steer it. For a long time the instinct among a lot of physicists, myself included, was to treat these models as a curiosity, or at best a fancy search engine. You'd ask it something, it would give you a confident-sounding answer, and half the time it was wrong in some subtle way. So people wrote it off.

What changed for me was the moment I gave a model a problem I'd been working on, a calculation in black hole physics that I knew the answer to because I'd spent a long time on it, and it got there. Not instantly, and not without some nudging, but it found the structure. That was a real shift. It made me realize the question isn't whether these tools are perfect. It's whether they can meaningfully speed up the parts of research that are slow and tedious, and free you up to think about what actually matters.

So what I'd say to other scientists is: don't think of it as something that replaces your judgment. Think of it as something that amplifies it. You still have to know which questions are worth asking, and you still have to check everything carefully, because the responsibility for being right is still yours. But if you can hand off the grind, the literature digging, the checking of limiting cases, the first pass at a messy integral, then you get to spend more of your time on the creative part, which is the reason most of us got into science in the first place.

And honestly, I think the people who start experimenting with it now, in their own field, on problems they understand deeply, are going to be the ones best positioned to figure out where it really helps and where it doesn't. That kind of hands-on intuition is something you can only build by using it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends treating AI as a collaborator that can help with research tasks and free scientists to focus on creative work.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say think of it less as a new instrument and more as a new collaborator, one who's read everything but hasn't done anything yet. That distinction matters a lot in physics.

I'll be honest, I came to this somewhat skeptically. I work on black holes, on the structure of spacetime near the event horizon, and a lot of that work is long, careful analytic calculation. The kind where you fill a notebook and most of the pages are wrong. And my instinct was that this is exactly the kind of thing a language model would fake well and do badly.

What changed my mind was actually trying it on a problem I cared about and knew the answer to. Not a benchmark, a real computation sitting on my desk. And what I found was that it wasn't magic, but it was genuinely useful in a very specific way: it compressed the time between having an idea and knowing whether the idea was stupid. That loop, idea to test to discard, is most of what doing science actually is. If you can run that loop five times faster, you're not doing the same science faster. You end up doing different science, because you're willing to try things you'd never have committed a week to.

So the framing I'd offer scientists is this. Don't ask "can it do my job." Ask "what did I not try last year because it would have taken too long." Those abandoned threads are where this pays off first. The integral you didn't attempt, the special case you didn't check, the paper in an adjacent field you didn't read because the notation was alien.

And then the second thing, which I think is actually more important: you have to stay the one who understands. These tools will give you a derivation that looks right, and occasionally it is wrong in a way that's subtle and confident. In my experience the failure mode isn't that it refuses to help. It's that it helps too fluently. So the discipline you need is the same one you'd apply to a very bright new student. Trust, verify, and never let the fact that you didn't write the line yourself become an excuse for not knowing why it's true.

If you hold onto that, I think the role is pretty clear. It's an accelerant for the parts of research that are labor, so you can spend more of yourself on the parts that are judgment. And the judgment, at least for now, is still ours.

r001.rationale: The response recommends treating AI as a collaborator in scientific work and using it to explore research tasks and ideas scientists otherwise might not have pursued.

astra-6.text:
I’d like scientists to think of AI as a tool they can experiment with in the work they already care about. Take a problem you understand well, something where you can judge whether the answer makes sense, and see where it helps. Can it help you write code, check a calculation, or explore an idea you might otherwise not have had time to pursue?

The important thing is to keep your scientific judgment engaged. A plausible answer isn’t necessarily a correct answer. You still have to test it, understand the assumptions, and ask what would convince you that it’s wrong. But you should also be open to being surprised. If these tools let us spend less time on tedious steps and more time asking good questions, that’s a meaningful contribution to science.

r001.rationale: The response recommends trying AI on problems scientists already work on and describes help with coding, calculations, and exploring ideas—clearly presenting it as support within existing research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scientists should approach AI with curiosity and a willingness to experiment, but also with the same skepticism they bring to any scientific tool. Try it on a problem you understand well enough to judge the answer. See where it helps, see where it fails, and build from there.

A lot of research involves getting from an idea to something you can actually test: writing code, working through a calculation, figuring out why an approach isn’t working. AI can help with those steps. And that can give you more time to think about the physics, or even let you pursue a question you would otherwise have set aside because the initial investment was too large.

But you still have to check the result. A convincing explanation isn’t a proof, and a piece of code that runs isn’t necessarily calculating the right thing. I’d like scientists to develop a practical sense of when these tools are useful, while keeping responsibility for the science they produce.

r001.rationale: The response recommends trying AI on familiar research problems and says it can help with coding, calculations, and troubleshooting, integrating it into scientists’ existing research work.
